purpose: English retrieval evaluation for the Bhagavad Gita chunk corpus.
how_to_use: The retrieval system must receive ONLY the 'question' field. Do not pass gold_sources, expected_answer_summary, or gold_evidence into the query. After retrieval, score hits against gold_chunk_ids / source_record_id.

questions.question: What does Bhagavad Gita 2.47 say?
questions.expected_answer_summary: Krishna tells Arjuna he may do his prescribed duty but is not entitled to the fruits of action, should not claim to be the cause of results, and should not cling to inaction.
questions.gold_evidence: vad-gita 2.47 — Translation  You have a right to perform your prescribed duty, but you are not entitled to the fruits of action. Never consider yourself the cause of the results of your activities, and never be attached to not doing your duty.

questions.question: According to Bhagavad Gita 18.66, what does Krishna tell Arjuna to surrender, and what does He promise?
questions.expected_answer_summary: Arjuna should give up all other varieties of religion and surrender to Krishna, who promises to deliver him from sinful reactions and tells him not to fear.
questions.gold_evidence: Bhagavad-gita 18.66 — Translation  Abandon all varieties of religion and just surrender unto Me. I shall deliver you from all sinful reactions. Do not fear.

questions.question: In Bhagavad Gita 11.32, how does Krishna describe Himself when He speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield?
questions.expected_answer_summary: Krishna identifies Himself as time, the destroyer of the worlds, come to destroy the people there; except for the Pandavas, the soldiers on both sides will be slain.
questions.gold_evidence: he Supreme Personality of Godhead said: Time I am, the great destroyer of the worlds, and I have come here to destroy all people. With the exception of you [the Päëòavas], all the soldiers here on both sides will be slain.

questions.question: At the very end of the Gita, what is Sanjaya’s concluding opinion about where Krishna and Arjuna are present?
questions.expected_answer_summary: Sanjaya says that wherever Krishna and Arjuna are, there will be opulence, victory, extraordinary power, and morality.
questions.gold_evidence: Bhagavad-gita 18.78 — Translation  Wherever there is Kåñëa, the master of all mystics, and wherever there is Arjuna, the supreme archer, there will also certainly be opulence, victory, extraordinary power, and morality. That is my opinion.

questions.question: What does King Dhritarashtra ask Sanjaya at the beginning of Chapter 1?
questions.expected_answer_summary: He asks what his sons and the sons of Pandu did after assembling at Kurukshetra, wanting to fight.
questions.gold_evidence: image at Kurukñetra, desiring to fight, what did they do?

questions.question: If someone’s body is destroyed, does the Gita say the soul is destroyed with it?
questions.expected_answer_summary: No. The soul is unborn and is not slain when the body is slain; it passes into another body as it already passed from childhood to old age.
questions.gold_evidence: rnal, ever-existing and primeval. He is not slain when the body is slain.
questions.notes: Both 2.20 and 2.13 genuinely answer; 2.20 is the more direct ‘not slain’ statement.

questions.question: Why does Krishna say He appears in the world from age to age?
questions.expected_answer_summary: When religion declines and irreligion rises, He descends to protect the pious, destroy miscreants, and reestablish religion, age after age.
questions.gold_evidence: ation  Whenever and wherever there is a decline in religious practice, O descendant of Bharata, and a predominant rise of irreligion—at that time I descend Myself.
questions.notes: 4.7 and 4.8 are consecutive and both required for a complete answer.

questions.question: If a person offers Krishna something as simple as a leaf or a little water, but with love, does the Gita say He accepts it?
questions.expected_answer_summary: Yes. If one offers Him a leaf, flower, fruit, or water with love and devotion, He will accept it.
questions.gold_evidence: one offers Me with love and devotion a leaf, a flower, fruit or water, I will accept it.

questions.question: According to the Gita, who is seated in everyone’s heart and from whom do remembrance, knowledge, and forgetfulness come?
questions.expected_answer_summary: Krishna says He sits in everyone’s heart, and remembrance, knowledge, and forgetfulness come from Him.
questions.gold_evidence: Bhagavad-gita 15.15 — Translation  I am seated in everyone’s heart, and from Me come remembrance, knowledge and forgetfulness. By all the Vedas, I am to be known. Indeed, I am the compiler of Vedänta, and I am the knower of the Vedas.

questions.question: When Arjuna asks about nature, the enjoyer, and the field, what does Krishna call the body and the one who knows the body?
questions.expected_answer_summary: The body is called the field, and the one who knows this body is called the knower of the field.
questions.gold_evidence: he Supreme Personality of Godhead said: This body, O son of Kunté, is called the field, and one who knows this body is called the knower of the field.
questions.notes: Grouped TEXTS 1–2; gold must keep verse_start=1 verse_end=2.

questions.question: What three modes does the Gita say make up material nature?
questions.expected_answer_summary: Material nature consists of goodness, passion, and ignorance, and the living being becomes conditioned by these modes.
questions.gold_evidence: Material nature consists of three modes—goodness, passion and ignorance. When the eternal living entity comes in contact with nature, O mighty-armed Arjuna, he becomes conditioned by these modes.

questions.question: Which eight things does Krishna list as His separated material energies?
questions.expected_answer_summary: Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intelligence, and false ego — eight separated material energies.
questions.gold_evidence: Bhagavad-gita 7.4 — Translation  Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intelligence and false ego—all together these eight constitute My separated material energies.

questions.question: Does the Gita say we should focus on doing our duty, rather than trying to control how the outcome turns out?
questions.expected_answer_summary: Yes. One has a right to prescribed work but not to the fruits; Krishna tells Arjuna to act without attachment to results, and also not to refuse the duty.
questions.gold_evidence: rform your prescribed duty, but you are not entitled to the fruits of action. Never consider yourself the cause of the results of your activities, and never be attached to not doing your duty.
questions.notes: Supported by both the verse and its purport; both listed.

questions.question: In what way can a person’s own mind be their friend, and in what way can it be their enemy?
questions.expected_answer_summary: If the mind is mastered it helps the person; if not, it remains the greatest enemy. One must lift oneself with the mind, not degrade oneself.
questions.gold_evidence: his mind, and not degrade himself. The mind is the friend of the conditioned soul, and his enemy as well.
questions.notes: 6.5 and 6.6 are a tight pair; 6.26/6.34 are related but not required gold.

questions.question: What does the Gita mean when it calls staying calm in both success and failure a kind of yoga?
questions.expected_answer_summary: Yoga here is acting in one’s duty while remaining equipoised, giving up attachment to winning or losing.
questions.gold_evidence: Perform your duty equipoised, O Arjuna, abandoning all attachment to success or failure. Such equanimity is called yoga.

questions.question: Is it better, according to the Gita, to stop working altogether than to keep doing one’s ordinary responsibilities?
questions.expected_answer_summary: No. Prescribed work is better than not working; one cannot even maintain the body without work.
questions.gold_evidence: tion  Perform your prescribed duty, for doing so is better than not working. One cannot even maintain one’s physical body without work.
questions.notes: 2.47 also warns against attachment to inaction, but 3.8 is the direct comparison.

questions.question: Why might someone believe ‘I am the one doing everything,’ and what does the Gita say is actually carrying out the actions?
questions.expected_answer_summary: False ego makes the soul think it is the doer; the activities are actually carried out by the three modes of material nature.
questions.gold_evidence: rit soul bewildered by the influence of false ego thinks himself the doer of activities that are in actuality carried out by the three modes of material nature.

questions.question: What understanding of Krishna does the Gita connect with finding peace from material suffering?
questions.expected_answer_summary: Knowing Krishna as the beneficiary of sacrifice and austerity, the Lord of all planets and demigods, and the well-wisher of all beings, one attains peace from material miseries.
questions.gold_evidence: Bhagavad-gita 5.29 — Translation  A person in full consciousness of Me, knowing Me to be the ultimate  beneficiary of all sacrifices and austerities, the Supreme Lord of all planets and demigods, and the benefactor and w

questions.question: What kind of person does Krishna call very dear to Him regarding envy, friendship, and not claiming to own the world?
questions.expected_answer_summary: A devotee who is not envious, is a friend to all, does not think himself the proprietor, is free from false ego, and is steady in devotion is very dear to Krishna.
questions.gold_evidence: gita 12.13-14 — Translation  One who is not envious but is a kind friend to all living entities, who does not think himself a proprietor and is free from false ego, who is equal in both happiness and distress, who is tolerant, always satisfied, self-controlled

questions.question: When this Gita defines karma next to Brahman and the self, what kind of action is karma said to be?
questions.expected_answer_summary: Karma is action connected with the development of the material bodies of living beings, i.e. fruitive activities.
questions.gold_evidence: terial bodies of the living entities is called karma, or fruitive activities.
questions.notes: This edition also calls the living entity Brahman in the same verse; the question is only about the karma definition.

questions.question: What does this Gita call yoga when it talks about working without clinging to success or failure?
questions.expected_answer_summary: That even-minded, unattached performance of duty is called yoga.
questions.gold_evidence: attachment to success or failure. Such equanimity is called yoga.
questions.notes: Shares a gold verse with 015 but asks for the term ‘yoga’, not the pastoral advice.

questions.question: According to the Gita, who actually performs activities when a person, under false ego, thinks ‘I am the doer’ — and what role do the gunas play?
questions.expected_answer_summary: The three modes (gunas) of material nature carry out the activities; false ego makes the soul think it is the doer.
questions.gold_evidence: hat are in actuality carried out by the three modes of material nature.
questions.notes: Same verse as 017; this item tests the term gunas/modes rather than the conceptual ‘why’. Acceptable overlap of gold, different question.

questions.question: What does this book mean by prakriti when it lists earth, water, fire, and so on as Krishna’s energies?
questions.expected_answer_summary: Those eight items are Krishna’s separated material energies; the purport names material nature prakriti, energy of the Lord.
questions.gold_evidence: —all together these eight constitute My separated material energies.
questions.notes: The English word ‘prakriti’ is in the purport (as prakåti). Translation says ‘material energies’ without that Sanskrit label.
